analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on coal, oil, and gas emissions and spends the money on families and public needs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2014 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge companies a fee for the carbon pollution in coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, starting at $42 per ton of carbon dioxide and rising about 2% plus inflation each year until emissions fall far enough [S3]. It would also charge large industrial facilities for other greenhouse gases like methane and give refunds for capturing carbon or exporting fuels so exports stay competitive [S3]. All the money would go into a new American Opportunity Fund for low-income energy assistance, bigger Social Security checks, college aid, infrastructure, direct dividends to families, and transition help for fossil-fuel workers, with a public website showing what comes in and where it goes [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families would get the main benefits: the fund could pay for energy assistance for low-income households, supplemental Social Security benefits, college tuition help and student debt relief, infrastructure spending, and direct dividends to individuals [S3]. Regions with high energy costs and workers in fossil-fuel industries would get transition aid [S3]. Everyone also shares in the avoided damage from a carbon fee that rises until national emissions fall to 20% of their 2005 level [S3]. Renewable energy and carbon capture companies would gain a market advantage as fossil fuels got more expensive [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income families, seniors, students, renewable energy

how_it_helps.text: Puts a price of $42 per ton on carbon dioxide from coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, rising 2% plus inflation each year, so pollution has a cost instead of being free

Channels all fee revenue into a dedicated American Opportunity Fund that can pay for low-income energy assistance, larger Social Security benefits, college tuition aid and student debt relief, infrastructure, direct dividends to families, and help for fossil-fuel workers and communities

Charges large facilities for non-carbon greenhouse gases like methane and later adds a supplementary fee to cover escaped methane from coal, oil, and gas operations, so companies cannot avoid the fee by leaking methane
Refunds the fee for exported fuels and lets importers face an equivalent fee on goods from countries without carbon pricing, protecting American manufacturers from unfair competition
Requires a public website disclosing the amount and sources of revenue and every expenditure from the fund

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies would pay the fee directly, and much of it would be passed to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, electricity, heating fuel, and goods made with fossil energy [S3]. Because the fee starts at $42 per ton and climbs every year, energy costs would rise noticeably, though low-income households and high-cost regions would qualify for assistance from the fund [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise prices for gasoline, electricity, heating fuel, and goods made with fossil energy, and while the fund can assist low-income households, middle-income families would absorb much of the increase

The bill lists nine possible uses for the fund, from dividends to debt reduction, without locking in any share, so whether families ever see the money as cash back would depend entirely on future Congresses and appropriations

Border adjustments and methane fees would require the Treasury to build complex new measurement and enforcement systems, and the methane portion depends on a reporting program that would not exist until 2016

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a serious, fully designed carbon tax: it covers methane leakage, protects exporters and domestic manufacturers with border adjustments, and dedicates every dollar to families and public priorities with public disclosure. Its real weakness is distribution — the fee would raise everyone's energy bills, and the nine permitted uses of the fund leave it up to future Congresses whether the money actually comes back to households as dividends or gets absorbed elsewhere. The climate benefit is real but slow; the price increase would be immediate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill with Sen. Brian Schatz on November 19, 2014
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day
The Finance Committee held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, and no further action appears in the record
The bill received a single cosponsor and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and the industries that burn their products are better off, because no carbon fee was imposed on them. Households got no assistance, dividends, or climate protection either, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, spared any carbon fee

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators supported the bill and no Republican did; it never reached a vote, so no roll call exists, but zero Republican cosponsors on a carbon tax reflected a party divide on the issue.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges them a fee on every ton of carbon in their products, starting at $42 and rising each year, with a supplementary fee on escaped methane, directly targeting their products' core cost advantage. Ordinary people benefit from cleaner air and a slower climate, but also face higher energy prices as the fee is passed through.
A rising fossil fuel fee makes wind, solar, and other clean sources relatively cheaper, expanding their market. This runs alongside the public's interest in lower emissions.

The bill pays refunds to companies that capture and store carbon dioxide or use it in products and enhanced oil recovery, creating a revenue stream for the capture industry. Public benefit depends on how permanently the carbon is actually stored.

They would pay more for fossil-fuel inputs, but the bill refunds fees on exported goods and lets the government charge equivalent fees on imports from countries without carbon pricing, shielding them from foreign competitors. Border protection for domestic manufacturing runs alongside workers' interests.

Utilities would pass the fossil fuel fee to customers in rates, and their fluorinated gas emissions are largely exempted from the non-carbon fee, easing their burden. The cost lands on ratepayers, cushioned only if the fund later assists low-income households.
